newsitem.title: USA: Clinton honors artists at White House dinner.
newsitem.headline: Clinton honors artists at White House dinner.

text.p: President Bill Clinton gave arts awards to actor Robert Redford, musician Lionel Hampton, playwright Edward Albee and 14 others on Thursday and honoured them further at a glittering White House dinner.
"At a time when forces seem so determined to divide us ... the arts and humanities unite us as a people," Clinton said in a toast to the group.

The black-tie dinner followed a ceremony at the Commerce Department at which Clinton presented the National Medal of Arts to 10 artists, an arts patron and the Boys Choir of Harlem and the Frankel Prize in the Humanities to five others, including Pulitzer prize-winning author Doris Kearns Goodwin.

"They are men and women whose accomplishments speak to the breadth and depth of our creative and intellectual genius," said a relaxed and genial Clinton, who joked with many of the artists before bestowing blue-ribboned medals on them.

Clinton singled out Redford as having moved beyond his career as an actor, director and producer to encourage the fledgling efforts of others through his Sundance Institute in Utah and its film festival.

"The most important thing to me about Robert Redford is that he could have been well satisfied to be a movie superstar but instead he chose an entirely different life," Clinton said. "For years and years ... he has supported and encouraged many young and emerging screenwriters and directors."

In addition to Redford, Albee and Hampton, Clinton gave the National Medal of Arts to opera conductor Sarah Caldwell, photograher Harry Callahan, theatre director Zelda Fichandler and composer and musician Eduardo "Lalo" Guerrero.

Others to receive the award were arts patron Vera List, choreographer Bella Lewitzky, composer Stephen Sondheim and author and illustrator Maurice Sendak, whose book "Where the Wild Things Are" is beloved by generations of children.
"His books have helped children to explore and resolve their feelings of anger, boredom, fear, frustration and jealousy," Clinton said.

"Hillary and I read 'Where the Wild Things Are" to our daughter scores and scores of times, and I can tell you he helped me to explore my feelings of anger, boredom, fear, frustration and jealousy," Clinton added, sparking laughter.
Clinton quoted Sendak as telling him before the ceremony began: "This is my first grown-up award."
Introducing lyricist Stephen Sondheim, author of the musical "West Side Story", Clinton remarked: "I feel that I should sing about our next honouree but I won't -- relax."

Clinton took special notice of jazz musician, composer and bandleader Lionel Hampton, maestro of the vibraphone, whose New York apartment, along with most of his belongings, was destroyed in a fire on Tuesday, saying: "We are glad to see Lionel Hampton here safe and sound."
A beaming Hampton, who is 88-years old and walks with a cane, was wearing new clothes donated by his friends.

Besides historian Goodwin, Clinton gave the Frankel Prize to poet Rita Dove, a native Arkansan like the president, political philosopher Daniel Kemmis, Latin literature scholar Arturo Madrid and television journalist Bill Moyers.
The prize commemorates the late Charles Frankel, a former philosophy professor at Columbia University and a senior State Department official.

The Harlem Boys Choir, which received the National Medal of Arts, began the ceremony with several songs, including Duke Ellington's "Take the A Train" and ended it with a rendition of "Amazing Grace" that had Clinton swaying to the music.
